visible.summary:
Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years), and PNG has extreme levels of gender-based violence generally — among the world's highest documented rates. Port Moresby and Lae are dangerous cities for everyone; tribal-justice dynamics and police brutality affect marginalised people severely. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and sorcery-accusation violence shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

For a visitor: the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation, which is among the worst in the Pacific.
visible.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General security conditions affect all travelers severely; criminalisation is the trans-relevant mechanism.

sources.claim: ADB publication landing page: 'Assessment of the Legal Status of Sexual and Gender Minorities in 17 Countries in Asia and the Pacific' (content dated 17 May 2024) lists Papua New Guinea among its 17 assessed countries, with keywords including decriminalization and SOGIESC inclusion; the fetched landing page itself carries no PNG-specific finding (full report required).

HRW commentary (27 Jan 2009): PNG violence-accountability climate — a mob stripped, beat with hot iron rods and burned a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station; provincial commanders recorded 50+ sorcery-related killings in two highlands provinces in 2008 with perpetrators rarely brought to justice; sorcery accusations (linked to HIV deaths) used to hide murders and mitigate sentences; police routinely take no action.

ABC News (8 Oct 2014): Hanuabada village on Port Moresby's outskirts is a safe haven for PNG's gay and transgender community — residents live openly, transgender people wear women's clothes in the street without retaliation, while in Port Moresby gay/trans people are commonly raped or beaten, sometimes by police (documentary maker Vlad Sokhin, who found the village while travelling).

The Guardian (13 Jan 2017) on HRW's annual world-report assessment of PNG: the government of Peter O'Neill has failed to protect women and children and to respond to corruption and police violence — 'police abuse, including of children, continues to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse'.

Guardian Nigeria (reprint): describes Hanuabada ('big village', built over the sea) as a pocket of tolerance where the gay community is accepted — set against PNG where sex between men is illegal and stigma/violence widespread (a 24-year-old gay man recounts being pelted with stones and bottles); campaigners say attitudes shift with exposure to the LGBT community.

visible.summary:
Botswana is workable for trans visitors — Africa's strongest judicial record after South Africa. The High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2019 (Letsweletse Motshidiemang v AG, upheld 2021); the Court of Appeal ordered the government to register LEGABIBO; and trans people have won document-change cases (ND v Attorney General, 2017). Draft 2024 constitutional changes even contemplate intersex rights. Implementation lags the rulings (SALC documents unsatisfactory compliance), social conservatism persists, and there is no general LGR statute — but the courts are a genuine protection, unique in the region.

For a visitor: decriminalised, functioning courts, moderate social hostility.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2019 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: Document-change rights exist only via per-case litigation (ND v AG 2017); there is no general LGR statute — resident-facing; implementation gaps documented by SALC.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: LGR requires litigation per-case; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: SALC, Digashu & Mmolai-Chalmers (20 May 2024): Botswana's precedent wins — 2016 Court of Appeal ordered registration of LEGABIBO (freedom of association, expression, assembly), a 2017 High Court ordered the state to change a trans man's identity documents from female to male (dignity and humanity), and the 2021 Court of Appeal decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct — yet implementation across Botswana and Namibia 'has not been satisfactory so far'.

Alta Advisory (18 Jun 2024): Botswana's draft constitutional amendment would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities; in June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep 'intersex' and 'same-sex' distinct. Civic groups criticise the wider review process, but the intersex provision signals momentum toward broader LGBTQI+ protection.

UN UPR outcome, 43rd session (May 2023): Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendations to repeal Penal Code Section 167 (same-sex conduct between women) and to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition — 'a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced' (para 570); abortion-decriminalisation recommendation also declined.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Botswana: general human-rights assessment (violence against women, prison conditions, San discrimination) - the LGBT section documents the then-criminalised status and societal discrimination.

LEGABIBO official site: Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation running advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health/HIV work (e.g., World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong), with Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources — a functioning, legally registered community infrastructure (registration won in the 2016 Court of Appeal order).

The Independent (19 Dec 2017): Botswana's High Court ordered the government to legally recognise a trans woman's gender for the first time — Tshepo Ricki Kgositau won a female identity card after a four-year legal battle (gender confirmation surgery December 2016), dedicating the victory to 'every single trans diverse person in Botswana'. A landmark for legal gender recognition in the country.

Human Rights Watch (24 Jan 2018): previewed the coming Botswana constitutional challenge to the colonial-era 'carnal knowledge' law (hearing set for March 2018) as one of the year's key LGBT court fronts alongside India and Kenya. superseded: colonial sodomy laws struck down 11 Jun 2019 (upheld on appeal 29 Nov 2021); trans legal-gender right confirmed 2017-22.

visible.summary:
Namibia demands real caution from trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 Digashu recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 High Court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (SALC). Windhoek has a small organised community (Equal Namibia); police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.
visible.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct technically remains criminalised under the common law (unenforced) — a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 legislative backlash signals trajectory.
visible.localsOnly: The earlier document-change court wins are per-case resident litigation; implementation gaps documented by SALC are resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Common-law criminalisation is unenforced but real; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Washington Blade op-ed (22 May 2024) by Daniel Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre: Namibia's Supreme Court in May 2023 ordered the government to recognise same-sex marriages concluded abroad under the Immigration Act, but compliance has failed — immigration officials tell litigant Digashu himself that the ruling covers only case couples (he receives a visitor's visa on every exit), and gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than 'all persons'. A hostile parliamentary marriage-bill response and misleading media amplified the non-implementation. Documents the enforcement gap between pro-equality rulings and administrative practice.

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - regional framework document; Namibia's courts have decriminalised same-sex conduct (2024) and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Namibia' (2017): constitutional analysis - Article 10 omits gender identity/sexual orientation but 'other status' should include them per the UN Human Rights Committee; section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 allows gender-marker changes on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and 'not problematic' per the Legal Assistance Centre (2015).

Mambaonline (28 May 2018): Out-Right Namibia opened Namibia's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May (IDAHOT) at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. ORN director Friedel Dausab: 'It is a first.' The article notes the colonial-era sodomy law is on the books but not believed used since independence in 1990, and recalls 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommendations urging SOGI non-discrimination legislation.

Mambaonline (12 December 2018): dozens marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund on 8 December for LGBTI+ Pride — described as the 'biggest pride event' to date in Namibia. Dated evidence of a visible, tolerated public community presence.

Daily Maverick (26 June 2014): a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding (T-shirts, berets) but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original. Documents organised political hostility to LGBT rights in the record's political environment.

visible.summary:
Mauritius is workable for trans visitors — the Indian Ocean's most liveable jurisdiction. The Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct; the Equal Opportunities Act covers discrimination; and in 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan competed as the first trans woman in Miss Universe Mauritius — a public milestone met with national discussion rather than violence. There is no legal gender recognition law (a barrier highlighted by AfricLaw), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2023 decriminalisation ruling removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: No LGR law — resident-facing gap highlighted by AfricLaw.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and recognition gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: the Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct — advances noted for lesbian, gay and bisexual people with 'less evident' progress for trans or intersex people. No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised; Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex newborns may be registered 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act but nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned; legal gender recognition not possible and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Pride held since 2005 with counter-protesters; during the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and others used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

AfricLaw (23 August 2024, Lakshita Kanhiya): analyses the historic participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan — the first transgender woman in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024 — against the country's legal obstacles: the Civil Status Act of 1981 and Central Population Database as the framework denying recognition, plus pervasive stigmatisation, with activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G. Concludes legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate despite the visibility milestone.

US State Department 2016 Country Report — Mauritius: Section 250 sodomy statute almost never reached same-sex couples in court (sodomy references overwhelmingly arose in heterosexual divorce cases as an aggravating factor); documents societal discrimination, with LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and Young Queer Alliance, and harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing. Dated pre-2023 baseline for the record.

Young Queer Alliance policy brief (July 2021): 'Administrative recognition of Trans People in Mauritius' - argues for legal gender recognition; notes the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders (2019) and calls on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law.

visible.summary: Seychelles is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent archipelago with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence is resident-facing; evidence is thin given the tiny population.

sources.claim: Cornell Law gender-justice page: under the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) Section 5, protected characteristics now include sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status, giving an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences. The Constitution separately guarantees freedom from torture (Art 16) and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex (Art 27).

PinkNews, 18 May 2016: Seychelles repealed colonial-era Penal Code Section 151, which had allowed up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex sex - framed as the popular holiday destination 'opening its arms to LGBT people'.

Travel guide: notes the 2016 decriminalisation of same-sex acts as a significant victory for the islands, while advising both local residents and tourists to stay vigilant and informed about the current legal and social landscape - practical visitor guidance for the destination.

Erasing 76 Crimes, 27 September 2024: a newly revised law calls for increased prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward victims' sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability - per the Human Dignity Trust, after South Africa Seychelles is only the second African country to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation. Before 2016 the penal code punished male same-sex intimacy with up to 14 years.

visible.summary:
Senegal is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “unnatural acts” (up to 5 years, applied to both men and women), enforcement is active (periodic arrest waves), and anti-LGBT forces are pushing to raise sentences to 15 years. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented, and even public discussion is policed: two men were jailed in 2024 for “false news” after accusing the Prime Minister of tolerating homosexuality. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community infrastructure — Dakar's scene is deeply underground.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest and mob violence.
visible.tangentialFactors: “Unnatural acts” criminalised (up to 5 years, both sexes) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; mob violence is documented climate.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity (Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, up to 5 years' imprisonment). (Only the opening of the profile was retrievable at fetch time.)

76crimes (16 Jul 2024): anti-LGBT forces in Senegal are pushing for 15-year prison sentences for gay sex, up from the current maximum of five years — a debate running since 2020, with abuses against LGBT+ people commonplace in the West African nation.

BBC News: two men were jailed in Senegal for criticising opposition leader Ousmane Sonko — months and fined 100,000 CFA francs ($165, £130) each. They had been angered that Mr Sonko had allowed a visiting French politician to express his support for same-sex marriages. Homosexual acts are banned in the mainly Muslim West African country and are punishable by up to five years in prison. The political activist and the preacher were arrested two weeks ago after posting a video attacking Mr Sonko for giving a platform t

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Senegal: documents preelectoral violence, torture, and 'violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons' among major human-rights problems.

76crimes (24 Sep 2018): four LGBT people — two women and two men — were detained in Dakar for 'acts against the order of nature' amid a wave of politically motivated arrests ahead of the 2019 elections, triggered after videos circulated.

Metro (Nov 2023): a man's body was dug up and burned in the street in Senegal after it was revealed he was gay — exhumed and set on fire in the street after locals are said to have found out he was gay, in a case that has shocked the West African country. Four men have been arrested in connection with the incident, though images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathering around the fire.
